pedagogy.summary: At 7-8, repeated reasoning matures into working the multiplication tables as a web of derivable facts and checkable patterns: noticing all multiples of 4 are even and using that to CHECK an answer, deriving 8×7 from 8×5 + 8×2, and describing the rule of a growing sequence ('add 50 each time') to predict onward. The MP8 emphasis on 'maintaining oversight… evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results' becomes concrete here: a pattern (multiples of 4 are even) is not just noticed but used as a reasonableness check. Teaching should build tables from known facts and pattern, not rote alone, and always ask 'does that answer look sensible given the pattern?'
bestPractices: Derive harder table facts from anchor facts (×5 and ×2 to reach ×7) using an array split, so the table is a network not a list to memorise
Explicitly use pattern as a check: 'a multiple of 4 must be even — is your answer even?' to build reasonableness monitoring
Have children describe the rule of a growing sequence and predict several terms ahead, then verify
Surface and test near-generalisations ('all multiples of 4 are even — are all even numbers multiples of 4?') to sharpen what the rule does and doesn't claim
keyRepresentations: Arrays / area model split for deriving ×7 from ×5 + ×2
Multiplication grid highlighting column/row patterns (evens, digit patterns)
Number line with equal repeated steps for growing sequences (+50)
Hundred square shading multiples to reveal their pattern
commonMisconceptions: Skip-counts or guesses harder facts instead of deriving them from known ones (8×5 + 8×2)
Splits the derivation wrongly (8×5 + 2, forgetting to multiply the 2 by 8)
Accepts an unreasonable answer because the pattern check (multiples of 4 are even) isn't applied
Over-generalises a pattern from a few cases without testing, or reverses it wrongly (thinks every even number is a multiple of 4)

learn.summary: For ages 7-8, turn multiplication tables from a memorised list into a web of derivable facts and checkable patterns. Children derive a harder fact (8×7) from anchor facts they own (8×5 + 8×2 = 40 + 16 = 56) using an array split, use a pattern as a reasonableness check (multiples of 4 and 8 are even — is my answer even?), and describe/test the rule of a growing sequence ('add 50 each time') to predict onward terms. The core habit is deriving AND self-checking, plus probing what a pattern does and does not claim.

activities.title: Split an array to derive a hard fact
feedback: If a child skip-counts 8, 16, 24… or recalls insecurely: show the array split into 8×5 and 8×2 so the two anchor facts are visible to combine.
If a child computes 8×5 + 2 = 42 (forgetting to multiply the 2 by 8): return to the array — the second block is also 8 tall, so it is 8×2 = 16, not 2. This is a scaffolding nudge, not a full reteach.
activities.rationale: Deriving facts from known facts and using arrays that reveal structure supports reasoning over rote recall; a splittable/foldable array makes the decomposition something the child acts on.
sourceClaims: MP8: students notice repeated calculations, look for general methods and shortcuts (e.g. deriving facts), and maintain oversight by continually evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results
Pupils should derive facts from known facts and recognise/use mathematical structure; teaching should use representations (arrays, grids) that reveal the pattern and support reasoning
learnerActions: Face 8×7 shown as an array 8 rows tall and 7 wide.
Cut the 7 into 5 and 2 (drag a divider, fold a paper array, or draw a line) so the array cleaves into an 8×5 block and an 8×2 block.
Read off 8×5 = 40 and 8×2 = 16, then combine the two blocks to get 56.

Try a different way to reach the same answer: 8×8 − 8 = 64 − 8 = 56 (take one group of 8 away from eight 8s). Compare which way you prefer and why — this uses one fewer group of 8, which is a different idea from cutting the 7 into 5 and 2.
activities.intendedInsight: A 'hard' table fact can be assembled from facts you already own; the array makes the decomposition (distributive idea) visible rather than relying on recall or skip-counting, and the 8×8 − 8 route is a distinct alternative strategy (adjusting from a near fact), not another split of the 7.

activities.title: Use a table pattern as a reasonableness check
feedback: If a child has no test when asked to check: practise 'multiples of 4/8 are even; is yours?' and connect it back to the shaded grid.

If a child accepts an odd number as a multiple of 4: point to the shaded multiples of 4 (a single column or row on a multiplication grid, a staggered pattern on a 10-wide hundred square) — no odd number is shaded.
A product that is odd cannot be a multiple of 4 or 8; a product well outside the 40–64 range for 8×7 should prompt a recheck — then confirm the exact value by the derivation.
activities.rationale: Maintaining oversight by evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results is central to MP8; a shadeable grid makes the pattern visible so it can be used as a live check.
sourceClaims: MP8: students notice repeated calculations, look for general methods and shortcuts (e.g. deriving facts), and maintain oversight by continually evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results
Pupils should derive facts from known facts and recognise/use mathematical structure; teaching should use representations (arrays, grids) that reveal the pattern and support reasoning
learnerActions: Shade the multiples of 4 (and of 8) on a multiplication grid or hundred square and observe that every one is even.
State the pattern as a check: 'a multiple of 4 must be even — is my answer even?'
Apply the check to a proposed product: given a candidate like an odd 'multiple of 4', decide whether it can be right and say why.
Estimate before computing: 'roughly how big should 8×7 be — between which two facts I know?' (between 8×5=40 and 8×8=64).
activities.intendedInsight: A noticed pattern is not just an observation — it becomes a tool you use to catch your own errors and judge whether an answer looks plausible (this check shows an answer is plausible, e.g. even and within range, not that it is exactly right).

activities.title: Describe and test a sequence rule
feedback: If a child only continues one step: ask them to state the rule explicitly first, then jump ahead using it.
Check predictions against equal repeated steps on the number line; a term that breaks the constant step signals an arithmetic slip.
activities.rationale: Describing the regularity in repeated reasoning and using it to predict, then checking, is the sequence form of MP8.
sourceClaims: MP8: students notice repeated calculations, look for general methods and shortcuts (e.g. deriving facts), and maintain oversight by continually evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results
learnerActions: Given a growing sequence (e.g. steps of +50 along a number line), describe the rule in words: 'add 50 each time'.
Predict several terms ahead — e.g. the term after 350 (400), and the one after that (450) — then verify by stepping along the number line.
Say how sure you are and how you could check a predicted term.
activities.intendedInsight: A clearly stated rule lets you predict beyond what you can see and then verify, which is the predict-and-check habit in a sequence context.

activities.title: Test the limits of a pattern (don't over-reverse it)
feedback: If a child says 18 (or 6) is a multiple of 4 because it is even: offer the counterexample and ask them to list actual multiples of 4 (4, 8, 12, 16…) to see 6 and 18 are absent.
Correct distinction: 'multiple of 4 ⇒ even' holds, but 'even ⇒ multiple of 4' is false.
activities.rationale: Surfacing and testing near-generalisations guards against over-generalising a pattern from a few cases or reversing it wrongly; this is recognising precisely what the mathematical structure does and does not entail.
sourceClaims: Pupils should derive facts from known facts and recognise/use mathematical structure; teaching should use representations (arrays, grids) that reveal the pattern and support reasoning
learnerActions: Consider the claim 'all multiples of 4 are even' and agree it is true.
Now test the reverse: 'is every even number a multiple of 4?' Try 6 — it is even but not a multiple of 4.
State precisely what the rule claims and what it does not (every multiple of 4 is even, but not every even number is a multiple of 4).
activities.intendedInsight: A true pattern often does not reverse; testing a near-generalisation with a counterexample sharpens exactly what a rule does and doesn't claim.

activities.title: Check understanding with targeted questions
feedback: Include an '8×5 + 2' distractor for the split: the correct combination is 8×5 + 8×2, so the second term is 16, not 2 (giving 56, not 42).
For the sorting task, an even number that is not a multiple of 4 (like 6) tests whether the child over-reverses the pattern.
Pair each selection with a 'why' so recognition is backed by reasoning, not guessing.
activities.rationale: At this age, well-designed questions can probe the derivation and reasonableness-checking content when paired with a justification step; note this checks recognition and stated reasoning, not independent construction, so pair it with open construction tasks.
sourceClaims: MP8: students notice repeated calculations, look for general methods and shortcuts (e.g. deriving facts), and maintain oversight by continually evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results
learnerActions: Answer 'which known facts can you combine to make 8×7?' and explain why your choice works.
Sort a set of numbers into multiples of 4 and not-multiples-of-4, including an even non-multiple to catch over-generalising.
Spot the unreasonable answer: given candidate products, identify one that breaks a pattern (e.g. an odd 'multiple of 8') and say which pattern it breaks.
activities.intendedInsight: Questions can check both the derivation route and the pattern-as-check habit, including whether a child is fooled by a plausible wrong split; this checks recognition and stated reasoning, not whether the child can construct the derivation unprompted.

constraints: Build tables from known facts and visible pattern, not rote memorisation alone; always ask 'does that answer look sensible given the pattern?'

Arrays and grids should be things the child acts on (cut, fold, shade) so the derivation and pattern are visible; a pre-split array or fixed shaded grid with tap-to-reveal annotations can illustrate and reference the method but does not let the child choose the split or test their own candidate answer against the pattern — treat it as a scaffold.

Recognition/selection questions check whether a child can identify a correct split or sort numbers, but do not by themselves require the child to construct a derivation unprompted; pair with a spoken or written 'why' and with open construction tasks.
Open discussion alone supplies nothing to split or shade; pair talk with an array, grid, or number line (a practical pairing, not a claim that talk cannot support reasoning).
These are flat number-and-pattern ideas; a 3D presentation is not needed and may add load — this is a practical note for this topic, not a universal claim about 3D.
Pattern-as-check establishes that an answer is plausible (e.g. even, within a range), not that it is exactly correct; keep both the derivation and the check.
Keep the 8×5 + 8×2 array split distinct from the 8×8 − 8 near-fact route; both reach 56 but they are different strategies (decomposition vs. adjusting from a known neighbour).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit (arithmetic): 8×5=40, 8×2=16, 40+16=56; alternative 8×8−8 = 64−8 = 56; both confirmed. Estimation bound 'between 8×5=40 and 8×8=64' is correct for 8×7=56. Sequence +50 from 350 gives 400 then 450.

Self-audit (pattern logic): 'all multiples of 4 are even' is true; its reverse is false (6 and 18 are even but not multiples of 4); 18 is not a multiple of 4. The '8×5 + 2 = 42' error is a genuine common slip and is used only as a diagnosed misconception, never offered as a correct option.

The original claims that 'open talk supplies nothing' and '3D adds load, not insight' were softened to scoped practical notes; catalog fit rankings are not evidence of comparative efficacy or necessity.

sourceClaims are exact copies of this row's two sources; neither establishes that any specific activity here was empirically tested, nor that questioning is a superior assessment method. Source 2 is retained for the near-generalisation activity only as structure-level support, not as direct evidence for converse-testing.

Editor correction: activity 1's alternative route (8×8 − 8) was reworded into child-friendly language and kept clearly distinct from the 5+2 array decomposition (a near-fact adjustment, not a split of the 7).

probeDeeper: Ask 'could you also get 8×7 from 8×8 minus 8? which route do you prefer and why?' to test flexible reuse of anchor facts
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'all multiples of 4 are even — so is every even number a multiple of 4? what about 6?' to check the child does not over-reverse the pattern
Ask 'your sequence adds 50 each time — what will the term after 350 be, and the one after that? how sure are you?' to probe rule-based prediction
Ask 'without working it out exactly, roughly how big should 8×7 be — between which two facts you know?' to surface reasonableness monitoring
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for deriving 8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2 = 56, AND a reasonableness check such as '56 is even, and multiples of 8 (or 4) are even, so it looks right', or noticing it lies between 8×5 and 8×8. The derivation plus the self-check is the target.

errorPatterns.pattern: Skip-counts or guesses 8×7 rather than deriving it from the known 8×5 and 8×2
errorPatterns.nextMove: Split an array into 8×5 and 8×2 so the derivation is visible; connect it to the distributive idea they can see
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child counts 8, 16, 24… or recalls insecurely rather than combining the two anchor facts

errorPatterns.pattern: Splits the derivation wrongly — computes 8×5 + 2 (forgets to multiply the 2 by 8)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the array: the second block is 8 tall too, so it is 8×2=16, not 2; a scaffold not a reteach
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives 42, having added 2 rather than 8×2

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not apply a pattern as a reasonableness check, accepting an odd or wildly-off product; or over-generalises (thinks every even number is a multiple of 4)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Practise pattern-as-check ('multiples of 4/8 are even; is yours?') and test the reverse claim with counterexamples (6 is even but not a multiple of 4) so the rule's limits are clear
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked to check, the child has no test, or claims 18 is a multiple of 4 because it is even

responseLevels.gap: Skip-counts or guesses harder facts, mis-splits derivations, and applies no reasonableness check; patterns noticed but not used
responseLevels.full: Derives 8×7 from known facts, checks it against a pattern (even/between anchors), and states and tests a sequence rule — maintaining oversight of reasonableness and transferring the derive-and-check habit unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Derives a fact from anchors or states a pattern when prompted, but does not spontaneously check reasonableness or test/limit a generalisation

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You're sure that 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16. Use those to work out 8 × 7 without counting up in eights. Then — how could you quickly check your answer looks sensible?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reaching 56 by skip-counting shows no repeated-reasoning insight; deriving it from anchor facts AND checking it against a pattern does. A child with the habit both decomposes and monitors reasonableness; a child without either counts up or accepts an answer with no check.
